pairs.en: **1 Corinthians 15:1-2.**

*"Now I make known unto you, brethren, the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye received, wherein also ye stand; by which also ye are saved: in what words I preached it unto you."* [1 Corinthians 15:1-2]

Having finished the discourse of spiritual gifts, Paul passes to that which is of all most necessary — the subject of the resurrection. For here too the Corinthians were greatly unsound. And as in men's bodies, when a fever lays hold of the solid parts — the nerves, the veins, the primary elements — the mischief becomes incurable unless it receives much attention, so it was here too: the disease was proceeding to the very elements of godliness. That is why Paul now uses such earnestness. This was no longer a discourse about morals, about one man's being a fornicator or another's covetousness; it concerned the very sum of all good things. For touching the resurrection itself they were at variance. Since this is all our hope, the devil made his most vehement stand against this point — at one time wholly subverting it, at another teaching that it had already taken place, which Paul, writing to Timothy, called a gangrene. [2 Timothy 2:17-18] For if the devil could persuade them there is no resurrection of bodies, he would go on to persuade them that Christ himself was not raised, and that nothing he did was real. Such is the craft of the devil — never showing his hand plainly, but undermining like an enemy who tunnels beneath a city's walls.

sections.heading: Do you see with what modesty he begins?

pairs.en: So Paul first secures his own people, not by reasoning but by the plain facts they themselves had already received and believed — a thing most apt to shame them, since if they now refused to believe, it would not be Paul but themselves they disbelieved.

*"I make known unto you, brethren, the gospel which I preached unto you."* Do you see with what modesty he begins? He is making known nothing new or strange, only recalling to memory what had already been known and had merely fallen into forgetfulness. And in calling them *brethren*, he lays a quiet foundation for what follows — reminding them, even as he addresses them so tenderly, of the very bond by which they became brothers in the first place: the dispensation of Christ according to the flesh.

*Which also ye received* — not "which you heard," but *received*, as one receives a deposit entrusted for safekeeping, showing that it came to them not by word only but by deeds, signs, and wonders. *Wherein also ye stand* — he takes the ground from under any future denial, feigning not to know that they had been so tossed about, in order to win them gently. *By which also ye are saved, in what words I preached it unto you* — the very manner of his first preaching still stands; he does not need to teach the doctrine again, only to remind them of it, and so leave them no room to grow careless. And having said *ye stand*, so that they might not grow slack, he alarms them again: *If ye hold it fast, except ye believed in vain* — the whole contest, he implies, is being fought over the very center of the faith.
**1 Corinthians 15:3.**
*"For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received."* [1 Corinthians 15:3]

Notice again: not *I said*, not *I taught*, but *I delivered... which I also received* — establishing two things at once: that he introduced nothing of his own, and that what they had believed came to them by a chain of transmission, not by bare assertion. *For I delivered unto you first of all* — that is, from the very beginning, so that it would be the greatest disgrace for those so long persuaded now to change their minds. And what did he deliver? *That Christ died for our sins.* He does not say at once that there is a resurrection of our bodies — though this is exactly what he is building toward — but lays first a strong and irrefragable foundation by speaking of Christ's own death.

sections.heading: He died for sinners, being himself without sin

pairs.en: Here it is worth pausing over those who, infected with Manichaean error, claim that by *death* Paul means only our being in sin, and by *resurrection*, our deliverance from sin. Nothing is weaker than error — it is pierced through by its own words. For if this were so, and Christ did not truly take a body but "died" only in this figurative sense, then by their own logic Christ himself was in sin. But how then does he say, *"Which of you convicts me of sin?"* [John 8:46] and *"the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me"*? [John 14:30] He who dies for sinners must himself be without sin — and Paul does not simply say *he died*, but *he died for our sins*, both compelling the confession of a real, bodily death and signifying that before that death he was sinless.

Nor is Paul content with this alone; he adds, *according to the Scriptures* — making the claim credible and pointing to the kind of death intended, the death of the body which the Scriptures everywhere proclaim: *"They pierced my hands and my feet"* [Psalm 21:18 LXX], *"they shall look on him whom they pierced"* [John 19:37; Zechariah 12:10], and Isaiah's *"for the sins of my people is he come to death"* and *"he was wounded for our transgressions."* [Isaiah 53] Nowhere does Scripture mean, by our Lord's death, the death of sin — always the death, burial, and resurrection of the body.

sections.heading: Buried, and raised the third day

pairs.en: **1 Corinthians 15:4.**
*"And that he was buried."* [1 Corinthians 15:4]

This too confirms the former point, for what is buried is certainly a body. Here Paul no longer adds *according to the Scriptures* — perhaps because the burial itself was plain to all, both then and now — but he does add it again for the resurrection: *"and that he rose again the third day according to the Scriptures."* Why does he need Scripture here, when the fact of the burial needed none? Because the resurrection on the third day was, to most men, still obscure, and so he brings forward the ancient witnesses: the type of Jonah, three days and three nights in the whale's belly [Matthew 12:40]; the burning bush that was not consumed [Exodus 3:2]; the dragon in Daniel, burst asunder from within — each a shadow of the body that died indeed but was not held fast by death. And beyond the types, the plain words: Isaiah, *"his life is taken from the earth"* [Isaiah 53:8]; David, *"Thou wilt not leave my soul in Hades, nor suffer thy Holy One to see corruption."* [Psalm 15:10 LXX] Paul sends his readers back to the Scriptures precisely so they will see that none of this happened by chance, when so many prophets had described and proclaimed it beforehand.

sections.heading: He appeared — to Cephas, to the Twelve, to five hundred, to James, to all the apostles

pairs.en: **1 Corinthians 15:5-8.**

*"And that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to above five hundred brethren at once, of whom the greater part remain unto this present, but some are fallen asleep. After that he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. And last of all, as unto one born out of due time, he appeared to me also."* [1 Corinthians 15:5-8]

Having established the resurrection from the Scriptures, Paul now brings forward the living witnesses — the apostles and faithful men who actually saw the risen Christ. Had he meant only some spiritual deliverance from sin, it would make no sense to say *he appeared* to this man and that; this is the language of one establishing the resurrection of the body. He does not say it once, but again and again — *he appeared* to Cephas, *he appeared* to the five hundred, *he appeared* even to me. And of the five hundred: *of whom the greater part remain until now* — meaning, though I speak of things now past, I still have living witnesses. *Some are fallen asleep* — he does not say *are dead*, but *fallen asleep*, itself a quiet confirmation of the resurrection.

Why did Christ not appear to all at once? So that faith might be sown by stages: the one who saw him first, being fully assured, told the rest, and their report prepared the others to receive the sight themselves. And why to Peter first, though he had denied his Lord? Both because Peter had been first to confess him as the Christ, and so was fittingly first to see his resurrection, and also — even more — to comfort him after his fall, and to signify that he was not despaired of, entrusting to him first, before the rest, the care of his sheep.

sections.heading: Least of the apostles, and last to see him

pairs.en: **1 Corinthians 15:9-10.**

*"For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I labored more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me."* [1 Corinthians 15:9-10]

Consider the depth of his humility here. Having said *last of all he appeared to me also*, he is not content even with this — he adds, *as unto one born out of due time,* and then gives the reason: *I am the least of the apostles... because I persecuted the church.* And when he must, at last, say something great about himself — *I labored more abundantly than they all* — he does not even let that stand as his own: *yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.* On every side he finds a way to shrink the one lofty thing he was compelled to say. This is why he first sets down his own faults so plainly, hiding none of them, even that he persecuted the Church and laid waste the faith: so that, having shown himself truthful about what discredits him, he might be believed all the more concerning what does him honor.

sections.heading: Whether I or they, so we preach

pairs.en: **1 Corinthians 15:11.**
*"Therefore whether it were I or they, so we preach, and so ye believed."* [1 Corinthians 15:11]

A witness, to be trustworthy, must be shown to be a serious and credible man — and this is exactly why Paul first names his labors, so that he can now, without seeming to boast, number himself among the other witnesses and say: whether it was I who preached to you, or they, the message and your faith are the same.

Let us also, when we hear this, learn to speak openly of our own faults, and to say little of our merits — or, if we must speak of them, to speak of them with reserve, giving the whole credit to God's grace, exactly as Paul does here: branding his former life, while crediting his present state entirely to grace, so that God's mercy might be seen from every side — both in having saved him as he was, and in having remade him into what he became. Let no one who is in sin therefore despair, and let no one who stands in virtue grow overconfident; let the one fear all the more, and the other press on all the more eagerly. For neither can the careless man remain standing in virtue, nor is the diligent man too weak to escape from evil — as David shows us both ways: after a little carelessness, a great fall; and after being pierced to the heart, a swift return to his former height.

sections.heading: Grieve for sin, not for loss

pairs.en: Why, then, O man, are you cast down over lesser griefs, when even for sin — where grief has some real use — excess does much harm? If you have lost money, think of those who lack even bread, and you will find comfort quickly. If your body has suffered some hurt, remember that this is not yet the depth of human troubles — others wrestle with far worse. In everything, count not only what has happened to you, but also give thanks for what has not happened.

Look, too, at the man who seems richer, more honored, more powerful than you, and consider the anxieties hidden beneath his fine appearance — for wealth wears a cheerful mask over an inward gloom, while poverty, examined closely, often holds a quiet freedom the rich man never knows. And observe this too: give a poor man everything he thinks he wants — freedom from want, then abundance, then public honor, then high office, then a whole nation, then many nations, then the whole world — and his desire for something further will never be satisfied, because it is not his circumstances but his own thinking that must first be put right. The same is true in reverse: bring a great man down step by step, and if his mind is rightly ordered, he need not despair at any stage, for beneath every loss there remains someone worse off than he is, and a real good he still possesses. It is not wealth that founds pleasure, nor poverty that founds sadness, but the state of our own judgment.

Bearing all this in mind, let us build up a right cheerfulness against every unlooked-for grief — so that we may pass through this present life with peace, and obtain the good things to come, through the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom, to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, be glory, power, and honor, now and forever, and unto ages of ages. Amen.
